title: "HRS 2016 - Cognition classification using profile mixture modeling"
author: 
  - name: "Douglas Tommet"
    affiliation: "Brown University, Department of Psychiatry and Human Behavior"
  - name: "Richard N. Jones"
    affiliation: "Brown University, Department of Psychiatry and Human Behavior, Department of Neurology"

    address: "345 Blackstone Blvd, Providence, RI 02906"

date: '`r Sys.Date()`'
abstract: | 
  **Objective:** This analysis report describes the classification of cognitive impairment (Normal, Mild Cognitive Impairment, Dementia) using profile mixture modeling. The goal is to classify individuals in the Core Health and Retirement Study using data available in the (2016) Core interview, but to do in a way that (1) uses information learned in the HRS/HCAP study (Manly et al., 2022; Farron et al, 2025) and (2) produces a probabilistic classification for cognitive level. The approach we describe accomplishes these goals, remains consistent with the _actuarial_ approach to cognitive classification described by Jak, Bondi and colleagues and used in Manly et al (2022), but discards the classification tree approach for an analytically derived classification model. 
  
  
  **Approach:** 
  
  **_Step 1 - Data management:_** We manage data (define subsamples -- HRS age 65+ [n = 9,972], HRS/HCAP [n = 3,496], HRS/HCAP robust norms group [n = 1,787], HRS/HCAP validation sample [n = 50]), code analytic variables (cognitive indicators, self-report indicators, informant report indicators, HRS/HCAP classification results). No imputation for missing data, we're using maximum likelihood.

  **_Step 2 - Model calibration:_**  We fit a profile mixture model to the HRS/HCAP sample. We estimate two models in the HRS/HCAP subsample, each with a known-class mixture modeling approach that uses the HRS/HCAP classification results as the known class membership. The cognition model uses the 8 cognitive test scores of the core algorithm and self-rated memory, and is estimated in participants with at least 1 cognitive test score or a self-rating of memory. The informant model uses the Jorm IQCODE alone, and is estimated in participants with no cognitive test score who have an informant report. Together the two models classify every HRS/HCAP participant. Neither model uses limitations in activities of daily living (ADL) or instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), so the PMM and the core algorithm classify participants from the same information. Cognitive performance variables are regressed on the covariates (age, sex, race, ethnicity, education) with fixed parameter estimates derived from a preliminary model fit to only those individuals in the robust norms group. The cognition model has a general cognitive factor measured by the 8 tests, and class membership changes the mean and variance of the factor.

  **_Step 3 - Scoring:_** In the third step we fix every parameter of the calibration models, including the class proportions, at its estimated value, remove the known class membership, and compute each HRS/HCAP participant's probability of membership in the Normal, MCI, and Dementia classes. We refer to this as the _scoring model_. We compare the resulting classifications with the HRS/HCAP Algorithm, the HRS/HCAP consensus panel diagnosis (validation sample), and the Langa-Weir classification. Because the scoring sample is the calibration sample, agreement with the HRS/HCAP Algorithm is in-sample. Analysis A3_2 applies the scoring model to HRS Core respondents age 65 and older from 2016 to 2022.

  **End results**. A scoring model that produces a probabilistic estimate of membership in the HRS/HCAP "Normal", "MCI", and "Dementia" categories, and a classification (the most likely class), for each HRS/HCAP participant, with information about agreement with the HRS/HCAP Algorithm, the consensus panel diagnosis, and the Langa-Weir classification.
